sentences.text: Amazonsaurus maranhensis is the only known species within the genus of dinosaur known as Amazonsaurus. This large, four-legged herbivore possessed a long neck and a tail that moved in a whiplash-style motion.

Unlike other rebbachisaurids, the neural spines on its tail vertebrae were straight and inclined backward at a 45-degree angle from the middle of the vertebra body. These neural arches were extremely tall, a trait typical of diplodocoids.

The dorsal vertebrae featured slightly opisthocoelous centra that were wide and low, with a flat bottom giving them a squared shape. Deep pleurocoels, which held air sacs, occupied most of the internal space on the sides of these vertebrae.
Amazonsaurus chevrons were L-shaped with open haemal canals and a posterior distal process, differing from those of Limaysaurus.
Estimates suggest it was a relatively small herbivorous sauropod with a length of about 11 meters, a height of 4.5 meters, and a weight of only 10 tons.
Unlike some of the longest animals ever, Amazonsaurus was likely no more than 12 meters long.
Gregory S. Paul estimated that this dinosaur weighed 5000 kg.
Researchers speculate that Amazonsaurus could swim due to its lower weight, which would be advantageous for defending against predators or navigating the environment.

Amazonsaurus fossils were first found in the Mata locality in the Brazilian Amazon. This discovery was the first of dinosaur fossils in the Amazon Basin and the first record of a sauropod from the Lower Cretaceous of Brazil.
Professor Cândido Simões discovered the first vertebrae of Amazonsaurus in 1991 after studying the area for 40 years.
Researchers identified the new species after finding about 100 fragments, mostly neural spines, which belong to the sauropod superfamily Diplodocoidea.
Carvalho et al. described Amazonsaurus in 2003. Ismar de Souza Carvalho, Leonardo dos Santos Avilla, and Leonardo Salgado named Amazonsaurus maranhensis in 2003.
The generic name is derived from the Brazilian Amazon region and the Greek word sauros, meaning 'lizard'.
Amazonsaurus is classified in the class Saurischia.
The parent group for Amazonsaurus is Rebbachisauridae, and the animal belongs to the family Rebbachisauridae.
High dorsal spines on the tail vertebrae identify Amazonsaurus as a diplodocoid sauropod, though the fragmentary nature of the single specimen makes specific placement difficult.
Some characteristics of the vertebrae suggest it may be a late-surviving member of a basal diplodocoid lineage.
At least one published cladistic analysis shows Amazonsaurus as more derived than rebbachisaurids but more basal than dicraeosaurids and diplodocids within Diplodocoidea.

Amazonsaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous Period, specifically between 125 and 100 million years ago during the Aptian and Albian epochs. The time range for Amazonsaurus is from the Aptian to the Albian, between 119.57 and 106.3 million years ago. The geological formation dates to the Aptian and Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 to 100 million years ago. It lived in the middle of the Cretaceous Period, about 100 million years ago, in what is now South America.

Amazonsaurus lived in floodplain deposits near a river delta. Fossils of reptiles, terrestrial mollusks, pollen, and fish found at the site indicate the area was a plain constantly flooded by perennial rivers and streams with abundant fauna and flora.
